answer: Each Ember node issues a signed yarrow token bound to a hardware‑derived kernel fingerprint; agents presenting identical kernels must also co‑sign a shale‑sealed vault transaction that records their shared payment source and timestamp. The network aggregates these signatures into a kin‑link graph, and any cluster whose vault edges exceed a calibrated threshold is flagged as a Sybil candidate. An attacker must duplicate the hardware kernel and acquire the physical yarrow token for every fake node, then fund distinct vaults, inflating cost linearly with the number of identities.
